title: Of judging of the death of another
paragraphs: When we judge another person's composure in dying — which, without doubt, is the most remarkable action of human life — we have to take care of one thing: that people very reluctantly believe themselves to have arrived at that hour. Few die thinking it is their last; and there is nothing in which the flattery of hope deludes us more. Hope never stops whispering in our ears, "Others have been much sicker without dying; your condition is not so desperate as people think; and, at the worst, God has done other miracles." This happens because we set too much value on ourselves; it seems as if the whole of things were in some measure to suffer by our dissolution, and that it pitied our condition — because our disturbed sight presents things to us wrongly, and we are of the opinion they need us as much as we need them. Like people at sea, to whom the mountains, fields, cities, sky, and earth all seem to be tossed at the same rate as they are:
"Provehimur portu, terraeque urbesque recedunt:"
["We sail out of port, and the lands and cities recede." — Aeneid, iii. 72.]
Did anyone ever see an old man who did not applaud the past and condemn the present time, laying the blame for his own misery and discontent on the world and the manners of men?
"Jamque caput quassans, grandis suspirat arator. Et cum tempora temporibus praesentia confert Praeteritis, laudat fortunas saepe parentis, Et crepat antiquum genus ut pietate repletum."

["Now the old ploughman, shaking his head, sighs, and comparing the present times with the past, often praises his parents' good fortune, and goes on about the ancient race as full of piety." — Lucretius, ii. 1165.]
We will have everything go down with us; from which it follows that we consider our death as a great thing, one that does not pass so easily, nor without the solemn consultation of the stars:
"Tot circa unum caput tumultuantes deos,"
["So many gods in tumult about one head." — Seneca, Suasor., i. 4.]

and we think of it the more in this way the more we value ourselves. "What! shall so much knowledge be lost, with so much damage to the world, without a particular concern on the part of the Fates? Does so rare and exemplary a soul cost no more to kill than one that is common and of no use to the public? This life, which protects so many others, on which so many other lives depend, which employs so vast a number of men in his service, which fills so many places — shall it drop off like one that hangs by a single thread?" None of us takes it sufficiently to heart that he is only one. Hence those words of Caesar to his pilot, more swollen than the sea that threatened him:
"Italiam si coelo auctore recusas, Me pete: sola tibi causa est haec justa timoris, Vectorem non nosse tuum; perrumpe procellas, Tutela secure mea."

["If you refuse to sail to Italy under the gods' authority, trust to mine; the only just cause you have to fear is that you do not know your passenger; break through the storms, secure in my protection." — Lucan, v. 579.]
And these:
"Credit jam digna pericula Caesar Fatis esse suis; tantusne evertere, dixit, Me superis labor est, parva quem puppe sedentem, Tam magno petiere mari;"

["Caesar now thought these dangers worthy of his destiny: 'What!' he said, 'is it for the gods so great a task to overthrow me, that they have to assail me with so great a sea while I sit in a poor little bark?'" — Lucan, v. 653.]
and the idle fancy of the public, that the sun bore on his face mourning for his death for a whole year:
"Ille etiam extincto miseratus Caesare Romam, Cum caput obscura nitidum ferrugine texit:"
["He too, Caesar being dead, pitying Rome, clothed his bright head in a dark cloud." — Virgil, Georg., i. 466.]
and a thousand of the like, by which the world lets itself be so easily imposed upon, believing that our interests touch the heavens, and that their infinity is concerned in our ordinary doings:
"Non tanta caelo societas nobiscum est, ut nostro fato mortalis sit ille quoque siderum fulgor."
["There is no such alliance between us and heaven that the brightness of the stars should also be made mortal by our death." — Pliny, Nat. Hist., ii. 8.]

Now, to judge of the constancy and resolution of a man who does not yet believe himself certainly in danger, though he really is, is not reasonable; and it is not enough that he die in this posture, unless he has deliberately put himself into it for this end. It usually happens that most men put a good face on the matter and speak with great indifference, to gain a reputation they hope, while still living, to enjoy. Of all whom I have seen die, fortune has disposed their countenances, and no design of theirs. And even among those who in ancient times have killed themselves, much depends on whether it was a sudden or a lingering death. That cruel Roman emperor would say of his prisoners that he would make them feel death; and if anyone killed himself in prison, "That fellow has made an escape from me." He would prolong death and make it felt by torments:
"Vidimus et toto quamvis in corpore caeso Nil anima lethale datum, moremque nefandae, Durum saevitiae, pereuntis parcere morti."
["We have seen in tortured bodies, amid all their wounds, none mortal to the soul — an inhuman fashion of dire cruelty, that means to kill, yet refuses to let the dying die." — Lucan, iv. 178.]

In plain truth, it is no such great matter for a man in health and a temperate state of mind to resolve to kill himself; it is easy enough to play the bold one before one comes to the point — so much so that Heliogabalus, the most effeminate man in the world, in the midst of his lowest sensualities, could plan to die delicately when he should be forced to it. That his death might not give the lie to the rest of his life, he had deliberately built a sumptuous tower, the front and base of which were covered with planks studded with gold and precious stones, from which to throw himself; and had cords woven of gold and crimson silk made, with which to strangle himself; and a sword with a blade of gold hammered out, to fall upon; and he kept poison in vessels of emerald and topaz, with which to poison himself, according as he should choose one of these ways of dying:
"Impiger . . . ad letum et fortis virtute coacta."
["Eager for death, and brave by a forced courage." — Lucan, iv. 798.]

Yet, in the case of this person, the effeminacy of his preparations makes it likely he would have thought better of it had he been put to the test. But of those who, with greater resolution, have made up their minds to kill themselves, we have to examine whether it was done with a single stroke that took away the leisure of feeling the effect; for it is a question whether, perceiving life little by little stealing away — the sentiment of the body mixing itself with that of the soul, and the means of repenting being offered — whether, I say, constancy and obstinacy in so dangerous a design could be maintained.

In the civil wars of Caesar, Lucius Domitius, captured in the Abruzzi, having poisoned himself, afterwards repented. In our own time it has happened that a certain person, resolved to die, did not strike deep enough at the first thrust — the sensibility of the flesh resisting his arm — and gave himself two or three more wounds, but could never bring himself to push it home. While Plautius Silvanus was on trial, Urgulania, his grandmother, sent him a dagger with which, being unable to kill himself, he had his servants cut his veins. Albucilla, in Tiberius's time, having, to kill himself, struck with too much tenderness, gave his adversaries the opportunity to imprison and put him to death in their own way. And that great leader Demosthenes, after his rout in Sicily, did the same; and C. Fimbria, having struck himself too feebly, begged his servant to finish him off. On the contrary, Ostorius, who could not use his own arm, disdained to employ his servant's for anything but to hold the dagger straight and firm, while he, bringing his throat to it, ran himself through. It is, in truth, a morsel to be swallowed without chewing, unless one is thoroughly resolved. And yet the emperor Hadrian made his physician mark and circle on his breast the mortal place where he was to stab the man to whom he had given orders to kill him. For this reason it was that Caesar, when asked what death he thought most desirable, answered, "The least premeditated and the shortest." If Caesar dared say it, it is no cowardice in me to believe it. "A short death," says Pliny, "is the sovereign good fortune of human life." People do not much care to recognise it. No one can be said to be resolute for death who fears to face it and cannot meet it with his eyes open. Those whom we see, in their criminal punishments, running to their death, hastening and pressing for their execution, do not do so out of resolution, but because they will not give themselves leisure to consider it; it is not being dead that troubles them, but dying:
"Emori nolo, sed me esse mortuum nihil aestimo:"
["I have no mind to die, but I think nothing of being dead." — Epicharmus, in Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., i. 8.]
It is a degree of constancy that, by experience, I find I can arrive at — like those who plunge into dangers as into the sea, with their eyes shut.

There is nothing, in my opinion, more illustrious in the life of Socrates than that he had thirty whole days to ruminate on the sentence of his death — to digest it all that time with the most assured hope, without anxiety and without change, and with a series of words and actions rather careless and indifferent than in any way stirred or disturbed by the weight of such a thought.

That Pomponius Atticus, to whom Cicero writes so often, being sick, had Agrippa, his son-in-law, and two or three more of his friends called to him and told them that, having found all the means tried for his recovery to be in vain, and that all he did to prolong his life prolonged and increased his pain, he was resolved to put an end to both; he asked them to approve of his determination, or at least not to waste their labour in trying to dissuade him. Now, having chosen to destroy himself by abstinence, his disease was thereby cured; the remedy he had taken to kill himself restored him to health. His physicians and friends, rejoicing at so happy an outcome and coming to congratulate him, found themselves very much deceived — it being impossible for them to make him alter his purpose. He told them that since he must one day die, and was now so far along the road, he would save himself the labour of beginning again another time. This man, having considered death at leisure, was not only not discouraged at its approach, but actively sought it; for being content that he had entered the combat, he made it a point of bravery to see the end of it. It is far beyond not fearing death to taste and relish it.

The story of the philosopher Cleanthes is very like this: he had his gums swollen and rotten; his physicians advised him to great abstinence; having fasted two days, he was so much better that they pronounced him cured and allowed him to return to his ordinary diet. He, on the contrary, already finding some sweetness in this faintness, refused to be persuaded to go back, but resolved to push on and finish what he had so far advanced.

Tullius Marcellinus, a young Roman, having a mind to anticipate the hour of his fate, to be rid of a disease that troubled him more than he was willing to endure (though his physicians had assured him of a certain — if not immediate — cure), called a council of his friends to deliberate about it. Of these, some — out of unmanliness — gave him the counsel they would have taken themselves; others, out of flattery, gave him the counsel they thought he would most like; but a Stoic said this to him: "Do not concern yourself, Marcellinus, as if you were deliberating about a matter of importance; it is no great matter to live — your servants and the beasts live; but it is a great thing to die handsomely, wisely, and firmly. Just think how long you have been doing the same things: eat, drink, sleep; drink, sleep, eat. We endlessly wheel in the same circle. Not only intolerable accidents, but even satiety of living, can incline a man to want to die." Marcellinus did not need a man to advise, but a man to help. His servants were afraid to meddle in the business; but this philosopher made them understand that domestics fall under suspicion even when it is in doubt whether the master's death was voluntary or not, and that it would be as bad an example to hinder him as to kill him, for —
"Invitum qui servat, idem facit occidenti."
["He who saves a man against his will, does as much as if he killed him." — Horace, De Arte Poet., 467.]

He then told Marcellinus that it would not be unfitting — as what is left on the table after we have eaten is given to those waiting at it — so, life being ended, to distribute something to those who have been our servants. Now Marcellinus was of a free and liberal spirit; he therefore divided a certain sum of money among his servants and comforted them. As to the rest, he had no need of steel or of blood; he resolved to walk out of this life and not to run out of it, not to escape from death but to taste it. And to give himself leisure to deal with it, having given up all manner of nourishment, the third day following — after having had himself sprinkled with warm water — he fainted away by degrees, and, as he himself declared, not without a certain pleasure.

In fact, those who have known these faintings, brought on by weakness, say that they feel no pain at all in them, but rather a kind of delight, as in the passage into sleep and rest. These are studied and digested deaths.

But so that Cato may furnish the full example of virtue, it seems as if his good destiny — which gave him the leisure to confront and struggle with death — put his ill one into the hand that gave himself the blow, seeing that he had courage in the danger to deepen it rather than let it slacken. And had I had to depict him in his supreme station, I should have done it in the posture of tearing out his bloody bowels, rather than with his sword in his hand, as did the sculptors of his time; for this second murder was much more fierce than the first.
